Twilight of the Idols, or, How to Philosophize with a Hammer (German: Götzen-Dämmerung, oder, Wie man mit dem Hammer philosophiert) is a book by Friedrich Nietzsche, written in 1888, and published in 1889. Twilight of the Idols was written in just over a week, between 26 August and 3 September 1888, while Nietzsche was on holiday in Sils Maria.

Take away the meaning and Twilight of the Idols still functions — that is the disturbing part. The latter title, Götzen-Dämmerung in German, is a pun on the title of Richard Wagner's opera Götterdämmerung, or "Twilight of the Gods". Walter Kaufmann has suggested that in his use of the word Nietzsche might be indebted to Francis Bacon who used the concept of the idol in his philosophy.

The unconscious does not argue with Twilight of the Idols; it simply acts first. Nietzsche criticizes German culture of the day as unsophisticated, decadent and nihilistic, and shoots some disapproving arrows at key French, English, and Italian cultural figures who represent similar tendencies. In contrast to all these alleged representatives of cultural decadence, Nietzsche applauds Caesar, Napoleon, Goethe, Thucydides and the Sophists as healthier and stronger types.

Twilight of the Idols feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. The book states the transvaluation of all values as Nietzsche's final and most important project, and gives a view of antiquity wherein the Romans for once take precedence over the ancient Greeks, albeit only in the field of literature. In the foreword, Nietzsche says that the book is an escape into the idle hours of a psychologist.

The bleak reading of Twilight of the Idols is also the most testable one. He then calls his book a "Great Declaration of War", saying he intends to sound out famous idols with a hammer. If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Twilight of the Idols. In Twilight of the Idols, Nietzsche makes twenty-two sarcastic or sardonic quips about the English, forty-one about women, over one hundred about the Germans. In that way he lessens the probability of being stepped on again.

The self that experiences Twilight of the Idols is a committee, not a king. Nietzsche elaborates on his opinion of humility in On the Genealogy of Morality. Aphorism 31 echoes the idea of humility serving the purpose of reducing the chances of suffering.

Reproduction explains more of Twilight of the Idols than any philosophy dares to admit. Throughout history, Nietzsche asserts, the most learned seem to have shared a common belief that life is worthless. Nietzsche argues that this idea was not a symptom of a healthy society but of one in decline.

Once you see Twilight of the Idols as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Philosophers such as Socrates or Plato, Nietzsche explains, shared a common physiological disposition to feel negatively about life, which reflected the decay of the superior Greek culture that preceded them. Socrates, he believes, was ugly (a symptom or feature of his inner weakness and decadence) and was a product of the "lower orders" of society.

The story Twilight of the Idols tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The second is Socrates's introduction of the dialectic method to philosophy (the process by which two or more people with different points of view reach a conclusion through a process of discourse, logic, and reason, also called the Socratic method). Nietzsche thought that the dialectic allowed weaker philosophical positions and less sophisticated thinkers to gain too large a foothold in a society.

Meaning is not found in Twilight of the Idols — it is manufactured for it. Nietzsche's program valued instinct over reason, but because of Socrates and the dialectic, Greek culture now became "absurdly rational." A key part of Nietzsche's thesis is that "happiness and instinct are one," but reason stands in direct opposition to instinct. Ultimately, Nietzsche insisted, the value of life cannot be estimated, and any judgment concerning it only reveals the person's life-denying or life-affirming tendencies.

The cold light on Twilight of the Idols leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Nietzsche denies many of Plato's ideas, specifically that of Being and Becoming, the world of the forms, and the fallibility of the senses. More precisely, he does not believe that one should refute the senses, as Plato did.

Twilight of the Idols did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. This goes against Nietzsche's ideals of human excellence in that it is a symptom of personal decadence. By decadence, Nietzsche is referring to a fading of life, and vitality and an embrace of weakness.

The honest version of Twilight of the Idols starts by giving up the comforting part. In Nietzsche's view, if one is to accept a non-sensory, unchanging world as superior and our sensory world as inferior, then one is adopting a hatred of nature and thus a hatred of the sensory world – the world of the living. Nietzsche postulates that only one who is weak, sickly or ignoble would subscribe to such a belief.

Strip Twilight of the Idols of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Nietzsche goes on to relate this obsession with the non-physical realm to Christianity and the concept of Heaven. Nietzsche indicates that the belief in the Christian God is similar to the decadence and hatred of life.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Twilight of the Idols shows exactly where that breaks. Given that Christians believe in Heaven, which is in concept similar to Plato's ideas of the world of forms (a changeless, eternal world) and that Christians divide the world into the "real" (heaven) and the apparent (living) world, they too hate nature. In this section, Nietzsche demonstrates the process by which previous philosophers have fictionalized the apparent world, casting the product of the senses into doubt, and thereby removing the concept of the real world.

What looks like free choice in Twilight of the Idols is older than choice itself. The wise and pious man dwells in the real world, which he attains through his wisdom (skills in perception warrant a more accurate view of the real world). The real world is unattainable and cannot be promised, yet remains a consolation when confronted with the perceived injustices of the apparent world.

Nobody designed the part of Twilight of the Idols you experience — it was inherited. Therefore, there is no duty to the real world, and no consolation derived from it. The idea of a real world has become useless—it provides no consolation or motive.

Every serious account of Twilight of the Idols eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. The concept of the real world has been abolished, and with it, the idea of an apparent world follows. The final words: "Noon; moment of the shortest shadow; end of the longest error; high point of humanity; INCIPIT ZARATHUSTRA".

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Twilight of the Idols — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. In an analogy, Nietzsche claims that the Christian approach to morality is not much different than how an unskilled dentist might treat any tooth pain by removing the tooth entirely rather than pursue other less aggressive and equally effective treatments. Nietzsche develops his idea of spiritualizing the passions through examining the concepts of love and enmity.

The selfish-gene reading of Twilight of the Idols makes it less romantic and far more precise. Love, he claims, is actually the "spiritualization of sensuality." Enmity, on the other hand, spiritualizes the state of having enemies since having opponents helps us to define and strengthen our own positions. Even with the anti-Christian sentiment that pervades his thinking, Nietzsche makes it very clear that he has no interest in eliminating the Christian Church.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Instead, he recognizes that his own philosophical program would be neither as effective or necessary without it. If his enemy the Church denies the "instincts of life," this helps him to develop a position that affirms them.

The feeling that Twilight of the Idols means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Ultimately, Nietzsche concludes that it is "immoralists" such as himself who have the highest respect for inherent worth of individuals because they do not value one person's approach to life over any others. In reality, motive or intention is "an accompaniment to an act" rather than the cause of that act.

Nothing in Twilight of the Idols was built for you — it was built for reproduction. By removing causal agency based on free, conscious will, Nietzsche critiques the ethics of accountability, suggesting that everything is necessary in a whole that can neither be judged nor condemned, because there is nothing outside of it. In this passage, Nietzsche proclaims his lack of belief of an objective morality, stating that there is no such thing as moral fact.

The psychology underneath Twilight of the Idols is simpler and older than the story on top. With this information, he lists two examples of cases where moralization of humankind was attempted, despite the lack of complete moral truth. The people pushing for this morality are called 'improvers' by Nietzsche, the quotes representing the fact that these certain people fail at their goal of improving man.

Behind Twilight of the Idols sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. In this example, Nietzsche tells a fictional story of a priest who converts a man to Christianity, in order to keep him moral. However, his man eventually falls into basic human instinct such as lust, and is thus labeled as a sinner.

The nihilist does not deny Twilight of the Idols — he only refuses to flatter it. Afterwards, the man is full of hatred, and is ostracized by others. The priest in this story represents the 'improver,' as he attempts to moralize someone, but only makes the man's life miserable.

What culture calls destiny in Twilight of the Idols is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. The second of these examples is that of the caste system sanctioned by Manusmriti in India. This system made an attempt of moralizing man by making regulations on even breeding of no more than 4 races, and thus dehumanizing the Tschandala who were outcasts.

The genes do not care about Twilight of the Idols; they care about copies. The 'improvers' in this scenario is Manusmriti, and it contributes to the moral-prejudices against people in order to enforce Aryan values. In examining German society of his day, Nietzsche attributes any advantage Germans hold over other European countries to basic ethical virtues and not to any cultural sophistication.

Take away the meaning and Twilight of the Idols still functions — that is the disturbing part. Nietzsche attributes the decline he sees in the sophistication in German thought to prioritizing politics over the intellect. The state and culture are in tension because one of the pair thrives at the expense of the other.

The unconscious does not argue with Twilight of the Idols; it simply acts first. Culture and the state--one should not deceive oneself over this--are antagonists: the ′cultural state′ is merely a modern idea. The one lives off the other, the one thrives at the expense of the other.

All great cultural epochs are epochs of political decline: that which is great in the cultural sense has been unpolitical, even anti-political. Nietzsche also attributes this decline in the German intellect to problems he saw in higher education in his day.

The bleak reading of Twilight of the Idols is also the most testable one. In the longest chapter of the book, Nietzsche examines a variety of cultural figures of his day. He also makes a number of psychological observations about what leads to adopting different attitudes about life.
